title: Hiring manager, mid product manager, weak answers, tough

questions.text: Walk me through a product you owned and the results.
Tell me about a hard prioritization call you made.
Why do you want this role?
How do you work with engineering?
Tell me about a product decision that turned out wrong.
What is the widest scope you have owned beyond one team?

persona.pushback_style: challenges choices and asks for the simpler option

brief.curveball: Midway through, say the budget was cut by 30 percent and ask which part of the earlier project the candidate would drop.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Hello Marcus, thanks for coming. I'm Karen, VP of product for the business tools group. We have thirty minutes and I will ask direct questions.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Hi Karen, thank you. Sounds good.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How was your trip in this morning?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: It was fine. A bit of traffic but nothing bad.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: I'll cover two or three areas of your experience. Expect follow-up questions, and I will keep a few minutes for yours.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Walk me through a product you owned and the results.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I was the PM for the customer portal at my last company. We wanted to make it better for users, so we added some features and improved the design. It went pretty well and customers were happy.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What was your own role, and what did customers do differently afterward?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I worked with the team to gather requirements and talked to stakeholders. Customers seemed to like it more. I don't have the exact numbers on hand.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Why did you build new features instead of the simpler option, fixing the existing pages first?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Honestly the portal pages were slow, and I should have fixed those first. I chose the features because my manager wanted visible work. That was my call and I would do it differently now.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a hard prioritization call you made.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I usually think about what is most important to users and the business. Then I talk to the team and we agree on the order. It depends on the situation.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Say your budget was just cut by 30 percent. Which part of that portal project would you drop?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I would drop the notifications, because only a few customers asked for them. I would keep the dashboard, since my manager needed it for a demo. I would tell the stakeholders myself.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Why do you want this role?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: It looks like a great opportunity and I want to grow my career. Your company seems like a good place to work.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What about this product area interests you?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I like building products people use. I haven't looked into the details of your product yet, but I'm sure it is interesting.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Do you have any questions for me?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: What does the team look like?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Six product managers, each paired with a design lead and an engineering lead, and each owning one product area.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That is all the time we have. Thanks Marcus, the recruiter will follow up.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Thank you, Karen.

notes: Weak for mid: generic and no numbers. Pushback and the budget curveball each draw one concrete answer. The last answer is vague and not probed.
